scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Wari: The Dance of Huari's Sacred Rain Ritual
This is Wari. 16th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Wari · Peru · 16th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Wari originates from the district of Huari in Peru's Áncash region, rooted in a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita celebrating the first rains.
It evolved through syncretism with Spanish colonial religious festivals like the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary.
The dance was recorded in 1570 by Cristóbal de Molina as Waritaki, reflecting its cultural transformation.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed during the Virgin of the Rosary festival, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in Huari, and occasionally the Virgin of the Assumption in Chacas.
The dance marks the agricultural cycle's start of rains and reflects syncretism between indigenous and Christian traditions, embodying devotion and penitence.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians, sometimes eight dancers plus a captain in urban areas.
The choreography has three main moments: circular formations with rhythmic support on the fourth beat, a light step called arrebato, and a strong zapateo foot stamping ending the dance.
Dancers move in circles, emphasizing rhythmic footwork and coordinated group patterns.
Watch for Arrebato, Zapateo.

Formation: Circular formation with four to eight dancers, moving together in coordinated patterns

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is played by two cajeros using the pinkullo flute and wanqar drum.
The pinkullo is a wooden flute with four holes played with the left hand, made from waroma wood.
Listen for the pinkullo flute, wanqar drum.
The pulse is not explicitly described, implied steady rhythmic pattern with emphasis on fourth beat.

The music features a wooden pinkullo flute with a clear, piercing tone and a large wanqar drum providing deep, resonant beats. The rhythm emphasizes the fourth beat, creating a steady, ritualistic pulse typical of northern Peruvian highlands.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by floral shawls tied across the chest.
Embroidered velvet sashes with golden threads are worn at the waist.
The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño, and the face with a pink mesh mask painted with facial features.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variants exist in Pomabamba province and towns like Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz, differing in choreography and musical tempo from the Huari version.
Descended from pre-Inca agricultural dances linked to the pocoy mita festival, evolving through Spanish colonial influence and Christian religious festivals into the current Wari dance.

Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Wari is shares music of Huayno: Wari's zapateo step resembles a huayno escape step; chuscadas played during general dances are a regional huayno variant.
Wari is variant of Chuscada: Chuscada is a dance and song genre of the Ancash region, considered a regional version of huayno, performed during general dances in Wari.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Wari is a ritual dance with penitential symbolism, performed in religious festivals and embodying devotion to the Cross; outsiders should respect its sacred context and not appropriate its masks or costumes.

wardrobe.from_sources: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by floral shawls tied across the chest. Embroidered velvet sashes with golden threads are worn at the waist. The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño, and the face with a pink mesh mask painted with facial features. Hats are white toquilla straw with colored ribbons and artificial flower crowns. Knee pads with 35-40 bells symbolize penitence. White gloves and a command baton with a dog head and leather whip complete the attire.
